title: Steve Jobs talks about the Library of Congress (1990)
speaker: Steve Jobs
content:
# Steve Jobs talks about the Library of Congress (1990)

**Source**: /Volumes/NvME-Satechi/steve-jobs.ai/Database_Steve_Jobs/1990s/Steve Jobs talks about the Library of Congress (1990).mp4

**Transcribed**: 2025-12-31 10:32

---

**Speaker 1**: My idea of a library is it's both a sort of a refuge.
**Speaker 1**: Uh-huh.
**Speaker 1**: It's just you know, safe, wonderful place with lots of leather.
**Speaker 1**: [Laughter]
**Speaker 1**: Cool supply or something like that.
**Speaker 1**: And at the same time, it's a uh dangerous place.
**Speaker 1**: Uh-huh.
**Speaker 1**: Intellectually, where you can find you don't know what.
**Speaker 1**: And some of the really pleasure of danger in a library for me is in the stacks.
**Speaker 1**: Mhm.
**Speaker 1**: When you're wandering about and you find things talk to you, their spines talk to you.
**Speaker 1**: Mhm.
**Speaker 1**: You see stuff that's next to stuff or a whole domain of of categories of books you didn't even know existed.
**Speaker 1**: You dive in there.
**Speaker 1**: And uh adventure happens.
**Speaker 2**: We're very privileged and we've had access to some pretty nice libraries.
**Speaker 2**: Still these libraries pale in comparison with the volume of information at a Library of Congress.
**Speaker 2**: Okay.
**Speaker 2**: So, I think what's going to happen is rather than we're not going to tear down our libraries, but we shouldn't be building too many more.
**Speaker 2**: And we should be augmenting the libraries we have with links to the Library of Congress.
**Speaker 2**: Then to put the entire Library of Congress in even the smallest town, all we have to do is run a network spigot into that town.
**Speaker 2**: And hook it up to the computers and we will have the entire uh Library of Congress at our fingertips.
**Speaker 2**: Information stored in electronic form will actually be fairly permanent.
**Speaker 2**: And um will be fairly easy to transmit from generation to generation.
**Speaker 2**: I think the Library of Congress is in a unique position to lead this charge.
**Speaker 2**: To rally the efforts, the resources, uh the leadership necessary to lead us into this new digital age of information.
**Speaker 2**: I remember the the video game phenomenon, probably all of you do too.
**Speaker 2**: What was the most interesting thing about the video game phenomenon to me was that within a few years after its beginning, kids and non-kids were putting in $2.5 billion dollars worth of quarters into these things a year.
**Speaker 2**: You can look at these things as games and dismiss them or you can look at them as very simple simulated learning environments.
**Speaker 2**: So, as an example in a simple pong game, the game is constantly telling you how well you're doing by how well you score.
**Speaker 2**: And so the more you learn the underlying principles, the better you score.
**Speaker 2**: So, the underlying principles in these in these in the case of most of these games were fairly fairly simple, but carry the concept much further.
**Speaker 2**: Imagine if the underlying principles were a sophisticated macroeconomic model of how uh France might have functioned in the time of Louis XIV.
**Speaker 2**: This type of simulation then becomes a little less uh trivial than the video game and yet the principles are still the same.
**Speaker 2**: And you can imagine what it will be like if we could use the historical material in the Library of Congress coupled with the interactive computer technology that we're developing to do these things.
**Speaker 2**: These simulations will become what most of our students are learning from.
**Speaker 3**: I think one of the the things that really separates us from the high primates is that uh we're tool builders.
**Speaker 3**: Now I read a uh a study that measured the efficiency of locomotion for various species on the planet.
**Speaker 3**: The Condor used the least energy to move a kilometer.
**Speaker 3**: And uh humans came in uh with a rather unimpressive showing about a third of the way down the list.
**Speaker 3**: It was not not uh too proud of a showing for the crown of creation.
**Speaker 3**: So, uh that didn't look so good, but then somebody at Scientific American had the insight to test the efficiency of locomotion for a man on a bicycle.
**Speaker 3**: And a man on a bicycle or a human on a bicycle blew the Condor away, completely off the top of the charts.
**Speaker 3**: And that's what a computer is to me.
**Speaker 3**: Uh what a computer is to me is it's the most remarkable tool that we've ever come up with and it's the equivalent of a bicycle for our minds.
